endpoint_ledger.description: Terminal yes endpoint for the forecast card: candidate_r is elected governor by the race deadline.

meta.important_question: Will candidate_r be elected governor by the election's resolution?

realization_criteria: Certified or otherwise authoritative election result shows candidate_r wins the 2025 New Jersey gubernatorial election.
Subsequent recount or adjudication does not reverse candidate_r victory by resolution time.

risk_flags.note: Initialization relies on limited qualitative scenario text without polling or operational data.
Public actors are intentionally masked/fitionalized to avoid direct real-person targeting.
Many process indicators may move without resolving the binary endpoint until actual election results.
Electorate and cohort counts are realistic placeholders inferred from scenario scale, not source-stated figures.
Presidential-party approval is named as a driver but no directional reading is provided at T0.

premises: New Jersey has a Democratic federal lean but competitive gubernatorial history.
The incumbent Democratic governor is term-limited, creating an open-seat race.
Taxes, affordability, corruption narratives, and presidential-party approval are plausible vote drivers.
A narrow Democratic win still resolves the forecast to no.
simulation_brief.summary: A competitive 2025 New Jersey gubernatorial race pits fictionalized Republican nominee Candidate_R against fictionalized Democratic nominee Candidate_D in an open-seat contest after a term-limited Democratic governor. Core pressures at T0 include New Jersey's Democratic baseline, issue salience around taxes and affordability, corruption narratives, national-party sentiment, and recent Republican overperformance relative to baseline. Terminal outcome is binary: Candidate_R elected governor or not elected governor.
uncertainty_notes: Source packet is sparse and high-level; no polling, fundraising, turnout, or scandal specifics are provided.
Candidate identities are partially masked; actor construction uses fictionalized public labels.
Recent Republican overperformance is described qualitatively without magnitude.
No explicit institutional disruptions or third-party candidacies are specified at T0.

sociology_baseline.description: Most partisan voters update within party-consistent ranges, while persuadables remain somewhat movable on high-salience local issues.
Turnout spikes likely if voters perceive race as unusually close or symbolically important.
Cross-pressured voters may withhold public preference while privately considering defection across party lines.
Partisan social sorting stabilizes core voters and slows broad persuasion outside issue-specific lanes.
Narratives about taxes, affordability, or corruption likely need repeated reinforcement across media and peer networks to shift marginal voters.
Party identity remains a strong anchor despite gubernatorial race-specific flexibility.
Issue salience may fluctuate unless refreshed by campaign events, ads, or news hooks.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: Democratic federal lean coexists with competitive gubernatorial tradition.
Term-limited incumbent removes full incumbency advantage and creates succession uncertainty.
Property taxes and cost of living are central voter concerns.
Ethics and status-quo critiques may shape challenger opportunity.
Presidential-party approval and national sentiment may spill into state race.
Republican results have recently outperformed the state's baseline, increasing perceived competitiveness.
